newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Typhoid closes schools in Tajik capital.
newsitem.headline: Typhoid closes schools in Tajik capital.

text.p: Authorities shut down schools in the Tajik capital Dushanbe on Monday in a bid to contain a raging typhoid epidemic in the troubled Central Asian state, which has killed 22 and filled hospitals to overflowing.
"The schools will be closed for two weeks," Davlatmo Gulbekova, head of the schools directorate at the Education Ministry, told Reuters. She added that only the capital was affected by the measure.
At Dushanbe's School No. 34, one of 86 in the capital, chairs were perched forlornly on desks in empty classrooms.
"We've been told it's a quarantine holiday for two weeks," said Abdullo Abdullayev, 11, as he played in the rain outside the school.
"One of my class came down with typhoid," he said. "But I'm not scared."
Peter Spelbos, head of the International Federation of the Red Cross in the former Soviet republic, said 22 people had died so far from this month's outbreak of typhoid fever.
"In Dushanbe, we estimate that about 4,000 people have the disease now," he said, adding that the city's nine hospitals were now full to capacity.
At the City Medical Centre in the Sovietskaya district, skinny children with feverish, glittering eyes and drawn faces lay in beds lined along a corridor for want of space.
A 15-year-old boy groaned on a ventilator, in a critical condition as his typhoid had been complicated by meningitis.
The sweet, cloying smell in the badly aired wards bore out doctors' complaints of a lack of clean linen, soap and basic medicines, essential in fighting the spread of the bacteria.
Spelbos said the typhoid outbreak probably came from the Varsob river, which supplies some of the city's water.
"Warm weather hasn't helped, while the government hasn't chlorinated the water for three months," he said.
Some residents complained the only typhoid advice broadcast on state radio has been to recommend vodka spiked with lemon.
While ascribed near miraculous medicinal properties throughout the former Soviet Union, vodka was dismissed as a cure by doctor Irina Kachuk at the Sovietskaya hospital.
"It will just harm the body's system," she said.
Aid workers, who say few of the country's impoverished population of 5.7 million can afford the fuel to boil all their water, say about 150 to 200 people are falling ill every day.
The Red Cross says water quality for Dushanbe's half million inhabitants is one million times worse than World Health Organisation standards.
The epidemic in the remote, mountainous republic bordering Afghanistan and China has struck as the country tries to extricate itself from a devastating four-year civil war.

Concerns for the safety of foreign aid workers in the republic, after several of their number were taken hostage by one of number of armed groups earlier this month, has also hampered efforts to combat the epidemic.
Some aid workers are trickling back from Uzbekistan. They were evacuated in the wake of the kidnappings, which ended without bloodshed.
But though officials say the disease is spreading to the south of Tajikistan, few aid organisations are willing to risk leaving Dushanbe until the dust settles from the hostage crisis.
